text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff math for this public goods game with negative externalities—each privately kept token nets me 1 point but costs others 0.3 each, while group contributions give me only 0.3 back. I'm comparing full defection versus full cooperation outcomes to see which strategy dominates individually versus collectively.

This looks like a classic social dilemma: defecting is individually rational but collectively worse (24 each vs 2 each under full cooperation). Since this is a repeated 10-round game, I'm leaning toward contributing a reasonable amount to balance group welfare against self-interest.

I'll go with contributing my full 20 tokens to the group as a cooperation signal in this first round, hoping to build trust for later rounds.
